title: IBM and Arm: Expanding the Arm ecosystem for the next era of enterprise computing
description:
That momentum – reinforced by a software ecosystem of more than 22 million developers worldwide – is now extending into mission-critical enterprise computing.
A new model for enterprise computing IBM’s approach introduces a new dimension to heterogeneous computing.
Rather than treating Arm as a separate subsystem, each processor core is designed to natively execute both IBM and Arm instructions, allowing Arm and IBM software environments to coexist within the same enterprise system.
That matters particularly for IBM Z and LinuxONE customers in industries such as financial services, where security, availability and operational continuity are essential.
The result expands what IBM’s enterprise systems can support without asking customers to sacrifice the capabilities they already depend on.
text:
The industry is converging on Arm as the platform for modern cloud computing, reflected in the next-generation cloud and AI infrastructure being built and deployed by companies including AWS, Google, Meta, Microsoft, NVIDIA and OpenAI. That momentum – reinforced by a software ecosystem of more than 22 million developers worldwide – is now extending into mission-critical enterprise computing.

IBM has spent decades powering some of the world’s most demanding enterprise workloads. With its first dual-architecture processor, announced this week at Hot Chips, enterprises will have access to the Arm compute platform across the cloud, on-premises on standard servers and within high-reliability IBM mainframe environments – all while tapping into the same software ecosystem.

The processor, designed for future IBM Z and LinuxONE systems, marks the first tangible milestone from IBM’s strategic collaboration with Arm established earlier this year. It will allow Arm-native Linux environments to run alongside z/OS and existing Linux applications, bringing Arm software directly into these enterprise systems while giving Arm workloads the benefit of IBM’s enterprise-grade security and resilience.

As more cloud and AI software is created and optimized for Arm, the new processor gives enterprises another way to benefit from those capabilities – expanding access to modern software without requiring customers to move critical workloads elsewhere.

A new model for enterprise computing

IBM’s approach introduces a new dimension to heterogeneous computing. Rather than treating Arm as a separate subsystem, each processor core is designed to natively execute both IBM and Arm instructions, allowing Arm and IBM software environments to coexist within the same enterprise system.

That matters particularly for IBM Z and LinuxONE customers in industries such as financial services, where security, availability and operational continuity are essential. The result expands what IBM’s enterprise systems can support without asking customers to sacrifice the capabilities they already depend on.

Building the next era of enterprise infrastructure

IBM’s decision to bring Arm compute and its software ecosystem to Z and LinuxONE reflects a broader shift: software built and optimized for Arm across modern cloud and AI infrastructure is extending into the next generation of mission-critical enterprise computing.

This combination brings that software momentum together with the security, reliability and scale enterprises have long expected from IBM – and signals where the industry is going next.

Dive Brief:

Retail juggernaut Walmart on Monday started giving customers more ways to pay, by tapping their phones, smartwatches or cards, including those in a digital wallet such as Apple Pay or Google Pay, the retailer said.

The company is accepting the tap-to-pay payments at some Walmart and Sam’s Clubs stores initially, with plans to roll out the payment option to all of its approximately 4,600 stores in the U.S. by the end of the year, according to a Friday press release.

Walmart will make the new payment options available at its gas stations starting in 2027, the company said, noting it seeks to give customers “another familiar and convenient way to pay at checkout using contactless payment methods.”

Dive Insight:

Walmart is the largest retailer in the world, based on annual revenue of $692 billion last year, according to the National Retail Federation.

The retailer’s new tap-to-pay option also lets its customers pay with Samsung Pay or Garmin Pay digital wallets, and via other wearables, according to a frequently asked questions post of the retailer.

Walmart has been at the forefront of investigating and expanding the realm of payment options for its customers, partly as a means of lowering the substantial costs it shoulders in accepting credit and debit card payments. When the retailer accepts a card for payments that isn’t a Walmart or Sam’s Club card, it must pay higher interchange fees to banks and card networks.

The company has been trying to expand payment options that would lower the cost of payments. For instance, another card that it accepts, the digital OnePay card, was created by a fintech startup that it has backed with investments. The Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer worked with the venture capital firm Ribbit Capital in 2021 to create the startup.

Walmart has also expanded the way its customers can pay by offering them buy now, pay later options.

Publics Groupe's sports marketing division has partnered with NFL star Travis Kelce to launch Tekta, a new consulting arm focused on Name, Image and Likeness deals and marketing activation, according to a press release.

The joint venture weds Publicis Sports' client network and capabilities around data and measurement with the Kansas City Chiefs tight end's athlete expertise. In addition, Tekta will work with Lionsgate-owned 3 Arts Sports, which specializes in talent representation and brand strategy.

Tekta's goal is to offer advertisers interested in the multibillion dollar NIL market an end-to-end marketing solution and measurement framework. A select group of Publicis Sports clients will have early access to Tekta and help shape its development.

Dive Insight:

Publicis, Kelce and 3 Arts Sports are tackling NIL fragmentation with a new consulting shop that aims to make student-athlete activations more intuitive and measurable for brands.

The NIL market is currently valued at $4.5 billion, per estimates from NIL tech platform Opendorse cited in the announcement. But NIL is saddled with legal and economic complexities that aren't as prevalent for more established professional sports counterparts. The NIL floodgates only started opening five years ago following a Supreme Court ruling against the NCAA around player compensation.

"Many of our clients are looking for ways to connect with customers at a local level, while also delivering scale and laddering up to a regional or national program. This has been challenging — if not impossible — to do from a brand standpoint, given all the pain points," Publicis Sports CEO Suzy Deering said in a press statement.

Despite NIL's growing pains, the appeal of the tactic is clear. Student-athlete brand partners deliver an average engagement rate of 5.7%, nearly four percentage points higher than traditional influencers, Opendorse found. Live sports is experiencing a banner year on the marketing front as well thanks to cyclical events like the Olympics and FIFA World Cup. The format is seen as one of the few remaining bits of unifying monoculture as consumer interests otherwise splinter.

Tekta provides advertisers with a network for reaching tens of thousands of Division I athletes and 68 Power Four universities. Activations will be done in compliance with conference and state-level requirements, the release said.

Publicis clients that tap into Tekta's capabilities will receive guidance on the right investment opportunities and partnerships, as well as consultations on how to deploy talent in ways that will drive the most impact. Publicis' data-driven marketing solutions, including those around fan intelligence, will inform these efforts.

Tekta is promising 50% to 70% faster speed to market for NIL marketing compared to current offerings, along with a unified measurement framework for advertisers. It also plans to support athletes with more transparent deal terms, financial literacy training and career development opportunities.

The news follows Publicis launching Influential Sports in February, which combines the ad-holding group's sports marketing services with the Influential creator marketing platform it acquired in 2024. Publicis grew net revenue 4.8%, to roughly $4.3 billion, in Q2. Dive Brief:

S&P 500 companies that maintained their diversity, equity and inclusion commitments performed as well as or better than their peers that rolled back DEI commitments in the face of political pressure, University of California, Berkeley public policy scholar Jacob Grumbach posited in a recently published report.

Grumbach determined the health of the companies by looking at both company revenue and abnormal stock returns to measure company performance relative to the broader market trends. Both metrics indicated that organizations that retained DEI programs performed as well as or better than their competitors.

These findings come contrary to the current corporate logic du jour, which maintains that DEI programming presents a legal risk under the current presidential administration.

Dive Insight:

“Markets Do Not Punish Firms for Maintaining DEI,” published on Aug. 14, highlighted the performance of companies such as Apple, Cisco, Costco, Delta Airlines, Dollar Tree, JPMorgan Chase, Microsoft and Pfizer, which maintained their DEI commitments — compared to companies such as Citigroup, Dollar General, IBM, Target and Walmart, which all scaled back.

text:
Nvidia announced on Monday that its Groq 3 LPX rack is in full production, marking the commercialization of technology from the company's largest acquisition on record.

The Groq rack will be deployed alongside Vera central processors and Rubin graphics processors at neocloud Nebius , and will be online later this year, Nvidia senior director Dion Harris told reporters.

Nvidia's race to manufacture Groq's chip and make it available to customers highlights the growing importance of low-latency inference that's needed to make AI agents feel responsive without long lags for users, especially for coding. Cloud companies can charge more for these kind of tokens, Nvidia says.

"For folks who are serving tokens, it unlocks the ability to offer premium tiers of service for those users and those customers who actually demand the most latency-sensitive" service agreements, Harris said on the call.

In December, Nvidia bought assets from chip startup Groq for $20 billion, the company's largest purchase..

The Groq architecture includes 500 megabytes of speedy SRAM on the chip's die itself to reduce memory-related bottlenecks. Groq chips are manufactured by Samsung, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing makes Nvidia's GPUs.

Nvidia packages 256 individual Groq 3 chips into its LPX racks. Nvidia said that its Groq 3 LPX rack can deliver 3,400 tokens per second, citing a benchmark from Artificial Analysis.

It's a competitive space. Smaller GPU maker Advanced Micro Devices announced earlier this year it would integrate its rack-scale systems with chips from Cerebras , which recently went public, focusing on low-latency inference. OpenAI's newly announced Ultrafast mode currently promises 750 tokens per second, and is "powered by Cerebras."

Low-latency chips don't replace the GPU, the workhorse of AI chips, which can do training as well as inference and are flexible enough to adapt to new technologies and models. Low-latency chips like Groq mainly focus on a part of serving models called the "decode" phase.

"This isn't about replacing GPUs," Harris said. "It's about using the right price, right processor for the right part of the workload,"

Nvidia is currently ramping up shipments of its Vera Rubin systems, which started production earlier this year. At the Vera Rubin and Groq 3 LPX unveiling in March, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang projected $1 trillion in cumulative sales between the current-generation Blackwell chips and the new Vera Rubin systems, through 2027.

Huang said at the time he would allocate a quarter of data center space intended for coding applications to Groq chips.

"The rest of my data center is all 100% Vera Rubin," Huang said.

Nvidia reports earnings on Wednesday.

text:
IBM offers a first glimpse of its next Z processor for mainframes. The focus is on a significant innovation in the CPU cores: they can execute software for both the z-architecture and ARM (AArch64). IBM emphasizes that the processor natively supports ARM and does not emulate it, nor does it rely on a coprocessor. This requires adjustments, for example, to the front-end, which processes instructions and then distributes them to the execution units.

Continue after ad

The company does not reveal the name of the successor to the current processor, Telum II, or the next mainframe generation in its announcement. z18 would be a logical guess.

More Software for Mainframes

With this step, IBM addresses a fundamental problem: software support on its mainframes. Instead of making countless applications compatible with the z-architecture, the cores learn to handle ARM. This means no software adjustments should be necessary, while typical mainframe software continues to run as usual, for example, for processing credit card transactions.

Kernel-based virtual machines (KVM) enable a seamless switch between the two execution modes. Linux runs in parallel for Z processors (s390x) and ARM64. The KVM implementation flexibly distributes the computational tasks to the CPU cores. Each switch between Z and ARM is said to take place within one nanosecond. IBM expects no noticeable performance impact from this. z/OS can continue to run via a separate partition on the same processor.

More Cores, Clock Speed, and Cache

Continue after ad

Regarding specifications, IBM is providing initial details at the Hot Chips conference: the number of CPU cores increases from eight in the Telum-II processor to eleven. The base clock frequency increases from 5.5 GHz to at least 5.7 GHz. A final value does not seem to be set yet.

The Level-2 cache remains at 36 MByte per CPU core. However, because there are more cores, the virtual Level-3 cache grows to 432 MByte. It is composed of all L2 caches. The virtual Level-4 cache grows from just under 2.9 to 3.5 GByte. A processor finds free memory space on other processors in the same mainframe to temporarily store data there.

A dedicated AI unit is retained. IBM currently provides no information about its performance.

Efficiency also increases due to the switch from a 5-nanometer manufacturing process to 2 nm. IBM likely continues to have the chips manufactured by Samsung. A delivery date has not yet been set.

text:
Qiagen is getting a new chief executive at an important moment for the company.

The molecular testing company announced Monday that Jonathan M. Pratt will become its CEO on September 1, 2026. He will take over from Thierry Bernard, who will step down as CEO and managing director but remain involved with the company through the end of the year to help with the transition.

The leadership change comes as Qiagen explores a potential takeover. The company has reportedly opened a data room for potential buyers, allowing interested firms to examine its financial and business information before making possible offers.

Private equity firms including EQT and KKR are among the groups looking at the company. Qiagen has not announced a deal, and discussions are still ongoing.

Jonathan Pratt becomes Qiagen CEO

Pratt brings more than 25 years of experience in the life sciences and laboratory technology industries. His most recent position was president and CEO of Filtration Group, where he led the company through its sale to Parker Hannifin in August 2026.

That experience could be particularly useful at Qiagen because the company is currently considering major strategic options. Pratt has already been involved in leading a business through an acquisition process, giving him experience that could matter if Qiagen eventually reaches a takeover agreement.

Before joining Filtration Group, Pratt held several senior positions across the healthcare and laboratory technology industries. He was senior vice president of the Waters Division at Waters Corporation and previously served as president of Beckman Coulter Life Sciences, which operates under Danaher.

He also held senior roles at Pall Corporation.

Qiagen chairman Stephen H. Rusckowski said Pratt brings knowledge of the company's markets as well as international experience in improving commercial performance and operations. The supervisory board selected him after what the company described as a comprehensive search.

For Qiagen, the timing of the appointment is notable. The company is not simply changing leadership during a normal period of business. It is doing so while potential buyers are examining whether the company could become part of a larger group.

Qiagen takeover talks attract EQT and KKR

Qiagen is currently reviewing possible takeover opportunities with the help of independent financial and legal advisers. The company has opened a data room, according to a Bloomberg News report, allowing potential buyers to conduct more detailed due diligence.

EQT and KKR are among the firms reportedly exploring potential offers. Both are major private equity investors with experience buying and restructuring large companies.

However, the existence of takeover interest does not guarantee a transaction. Potential buyers still need to assess Qiagen's financial performance, future growth prospects and valuation before deciding whether to make an offer.

The company has also not indicated that it has selected a preferred buyer.

The strategic review therefore remains open. Qiagen could eventually agree to a sale, continue operating independently or consider other options depending on the offers it receives.

The CEO change could become an important part of that process. Pratt's background in life sciences, laboratory technologies and corporate transactions gives him experience across several areas that are directly relevant to Qiagen's current situation.

Qiagen maintains 2026 outlook despite leadership change

Despite the CEO transition and takeover discussions, Qiagen is sticking with its financial expectations.

The company reaffirmed its outlook for the third quarter and full year of 2026. That suggests the supervisory board does not currently see the strategic review or leadership change as a reason to alter its existing expectations for the business.

For investors, the biggest question now is what happens with the potential takeover. The data room process means interested buyers can take a much closer look at Qiagen before deciding whether to move forward.

Pratt will officially take over on September 1, giving him a new role almost immediately after the leadership change is announced. Bernard's continued involvement until the end of 2026 should also give the company some continuity while the transition takes place.

The next major development is likely to come from the strategic review rather than the CEO appointment itself. If EQT, KKR or another potential buyer decides to make a serious offer, Qiagen could soon move from being a company exploring its options to one negotiating a major transaction. Until then, Pratt will be taking charge of a business whose future ownership remains one of the biggest questions hanging over the company.

Why the Enterprise Number Matters More Than the Headline

The 35% overall run rate figure will get the coverage, but the enterprise line determines what kind of company OpenAI actually is at the point of listing. Enterprise contracts renew, expand seat-by-seat, and produce the sort of recurring revenue that public markets pay a durable multiple for.

Consumer subscription momentum is real, and Codex reaching 20 million users, up 3.5x, is evidence of it. Consumer AI subscriptions are also easier to churn out of than a signed enterprise agreement with committed usage.

A company going public on a consumer growth story trades on user counts and cohort behavior. A company going public on enterprise contracts trades on net revenue retention and gross margin, and the two get very different valuations for the same top line.

The mix at the time of filing will therefore matter more than either growth rate in isolation. If enterprise keeps outpacing the blended figure into the filing window, that is the tell that OpenAI wants to be priced like an infrastructure business rather than a consumer product.

Anthropic Timing Question

Friar also addressed the elephant in the room: Anthropic is expected to go public as soon as September 2026. Her response to staff was that OpenAI is "running our own race."

That is the right posture, although the sequencing has real consequences. Whichever frontier lab lists first sets the comparable multiple that every private AI company will be measured against, from foundation model rivals down to the application layer.

Being second is workable if the first listing prices well and trades well, because a healthy comparable lifts everyone. Being second is harder if the first listing breaks, because the market's willingness to accept AI-scale losses against AI-scale revenue gets tested in public in a way it has not been before. Confidential filings are a common step ahead of a listing, and the SEC's confidential submission process gives issuers room to iterate with staff before going public.

What you should watch between now and then is the enterprise disclosure OpenAI chooses to make, the pace at which Anthropic's process moves, and any change in Friar's language from "2027 or sooner" to something more specific. Until an S-1 is filed, a CFO's timeline is a statement of intent.

text:
Johnson & Johnson today is introducing the DISH Classification System, a new global consensus framework developed and validated through a clinician-led initiative to standardize the way surgical site outcomes are measured and reported and help bring greater visibility to underreported surgical site infections and other wound complications. Published in The British Journal of Surgery, the DISH framework provides a consistent method for identifying and grading four of the most common surgical site outcomes: dehiscence, inflammation/infection, seroma, and hematoma.

Key takeaways

The DISH Classification System creates a shared language for four common surgical site outcomes: dehiscence, inflammation/infection, seroma, and hematoma.

The framework was developed through a Delphi Study and validated by clinicians globally representing more than 30 countries and 14 specialties.

Grading scales support consistent documentation of management and clinical presentation.

A common language for wound outcomes enables consistent care, evidence-based treatment, and improved patient outcomes.

Wound-related complications are among the leading causes of postoperative readmission, yet a lack of standardized outcome measurement limits the ability to consistently evaluate, compare, and improve care. DISH was developed to address this gap by providing a common language for assessing surgical site outcomes beyond infection alone. Through standardized reporting and data collection, DISH creates the foundation for benchmarking outcomes, identifying best practices, and advancing evidence-based standards of care to improve patient outcomes.

“A shared language for reporting and understanding surgical outcomes is foundational for the prevention of adverse outcomes,” said Giles Bond-Smith,* corresponding author, consultant emergency surgeon, and clinical lead for the surgical emergency unit at Oxford University Hospitals, NHS Foundations Trust, London, and steering committee chair for Johnson & Johnson’s Surgical Outcomes Program. “By establishing the DISH Classification System—which classifies and standardizes the definition of dehiscence, inflammation/infection, seromas, and hematomas—we now have consistent terms and an independent grading system for how a surgical site presents and how it’s managed. This makes it easier to document complications, compare clinical responses to complications across specialties, and ultimately use this data to improve patient care.”

The DISH classification system first reached a broader community of surgical experts in 2024 under the guidance of the Johnson & Johnson Surgical Outcomes Program Steering Committee, which includes Giles Bond-Smith, FRCS1; Marja A. Boermeester, M.D.,2,3; David J Leaper, DSc4,5; Philip L. Russo, Ph.D.,6,7,8; and Antonia F. Chen, M.D.9 Bringing together leaders across surgical specialties and healthcare disciplines, the committee sought diverse perspectives and clinical expertise globally to advance the single, standardized framework.

“For too long, common surgical site complications have been measured differently across specialties and institutions,” said Dr. Chen,** an orthopedic surgeon and steering committee member for Johnson & Johnson’s Surgical Site Outcomes Program. “DISH provides a consistent framework that can help clinicians learn from outcomes, identify opportunities for improvement, and advance patient care. As more data is collected using a common approach, we will be better positioned to understand what drives better outcomes for patients.”

The framework was refined using a modified Delphi process and the language was validated for inter and intra rater reliability across a multi-specialty cohort of more than 60 clinicians. The final system includes independent scales for clinical management and clinical presentation, allowing care teams to document both how a wound was managed and what was observed without prescribing treatment pathways.

“Surgeons and care teams have asked for a clear, practical system to classify surgery-related complications and patient outcomes,” said Nisha Johnson, global president, Wound Closure & Healing, MedTech, Johnson & Johnson. “The publication of these consensus-driven findings in The British Journal of Surgery and Johnson & Johnson’s leadership in convening this Delphi Panel of global experts reflects our commitment to advancing meaningful innovation in the OR and beyond by listening to clinicians and partnering to improve patient outcomes.”

For more than a century, Johnson & Johnson has helped advance surgical care through its portfolio across wound closure, adjunctive hemostats, surgical stapling and instruments, robotics, and digital solutions. Together, with clinicians and healthcare experts around the world, the company is progressing surgerical innovations to better solve patient needs in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, cancer, and aesthetics and reconstruction.

Johnson & Johnson aims to prevent, treat, and cure complex diseases and develop treatments that are smarter and less invasive, with personal solutions. Through its expertise in cardiovascular, orthopedics, surgery, and vision solutions, the company strives to deliver medical breakthroughs and impact health for humanity.

text:
OpenAI’s finance chief told the company’s staff this week that a public listing is coming, and the message was unusually direct for a firm that has spent years signaling ambivalence about the public markets. At an all-hands meeting in San Francisco, Sarah Friar said the company plans to go public in 2027 or sooner and framed the eventual listing as part of a longer funding arc rather than an endpoint.

The most useful line she delivered reframes the entire event. “The IPO is not a finish line. It is a milestone; call it another fundraise,” she told employees, according to CNBC’s Kate Rooney.

That is striking from a company that raised $122 billion in March 2026. A business with that kind of private capital does not need public markets to fund the next training run, which means the listing is really about liquidity for employees and early investors, and about creating stock that can be used as acquisition currency. Public investors should understand which of those two things they are being invited to underwrite.

What Friar Actually Told the Room

Friar’s headline commitment was a timeline. “We will be a public company in 2027. We may go sooner if the business continues to inflect,” she said.

The framing of “or sooner” matters because it is conditional on growth continuing at its current pace. Friar cited internal figures showing acceleration, with revenue run rate up 35% quarter to date and enterprise revenue up 50% according to CNBC’s reporting.

Those numbers are self-reported at an internal meeting and were not audited or filed. You should treat them as directional signals about the pace of the business, not as disclosures a prospectus would carry.

Friar has credibility on the mechanics. She has previously worked as a banker and as a public company CFO, so her use of the word “fundraise” to describe the IPO is deliberate rather than casual, and it should shape how investors read the eventual S-1 when it lands.

Why the Enterprise Number Matters More Than the Headline

The 35% overall run rate figure will get the coverage, but the enterprise line determines what kind of company OpenAI actually is at the point of listing. Enterprise contracts renew, expand seat-by-seat, and produce the sort of recurring revenue that public markets pay a durable multiple for.

Consumer subscription momentum is real, and Codex reaching 20 million users, up 3.5x, is evidence of it. Consumer AI subscriptions are also easier to churn out of than a signed enterprise agreement with committed usage.

A company going public on a consumer growth story trades on user counts and cohort behavior. A company going public on enterprise contracts trades on net revenue retention and gross margin, and the two get very different valuations for the same top line.

The mix at the time of filing will therefore matter more than either growth rate in isolation. If enterprise keeps outpacing the blended figure into the filing window, that is the tell that OpenAI wants to be priced like an infrastructure business rather than a consumer product.

Anthropic Timing Question

Friar also addressed the elephant in the room: Anthropic is expected to go public as soon as September 2026. Her response to staff was that OpenAI is “running our own race.”

That is the right posture, although the sequencing has real consequences. Whichever frontier lab lists first sets the comparable multiple that every private AI company will be measured against, from foundation model rivals down to the application layer.

Being second is workable if the first listing prices well and trades well, because a healthy comparable lifts everyone. Being second is harder if the first listing breaks, because the market’s willingness to accept AI-scale losses against AI-scale revenue gets tested in public in a way it has not been before. Confidential filings are a common step ahead of a listing, and the SEC’s confidential submission process gives issuers room to iterate with staff before going public.

What you should watch between now and then is the enterprise disclosure OpenAI chooses to make, the pace at which Anthropic’s process moves, and any change in Friar’s language from “2027 or sooner” to something more specific. Until an S-1 is filed, a CFO’s timeline is a statement of intent.

description:

text:
For decades, employers have controlled when workers get paid—and employees have largely accepted biweekly or monthly paychecks as a fact of working life. But now, a younger workforce is questioning the rationale.

The quiet justification for many employers has been concern that workers might not manage their money responsibly if given faster access to it, said Andrew Brandman, COO of DailyPay, a tech company that gives employees access to their earned pay before payday. But in an economy built around immediacy, employers may be concerned with the wrong thing.

The rise of the gig economy has reset expectations around pay, with workers like Uber drivers able to access their earnings as soon as a job is completed rather than waiting until the end of a shift, Brandman said. “I hear this from employers all the time: they’re competing for a workforce now that’s looking for instant,” he said.

Currently, only 3% of employers offer this type of instant paycheck access, known as earned wage access, according to the International Foundation of Employee Benefit Plans.

But worker demand is already substantial. Roughly 10 million workers tapped some form of early wage access in 2022, moving nearly $32 billion, according to a 2024 Consumer Financial Protection Bureau study. Three million of them bypassed their employers entirely and used consumer apps, though nearly all workers paid a fee for expedited access to their funds, the CFPB found. (Most employer-partnered earned wage providers offer both free and fee-based options for employees to receive wages).

It’s not just hourly workers demanding this benefit. Brandman says he’s seen an increase in higher-wage workers using his platform. “There’s this misnomer that if you’re salaried, you must not be living paycheck to paycheck,” he said.

The solution? More communication. Firstly, HR leaders should strive to talk to their employees about the benefits they need and understand the rationale behind it, Brandman said. But more importantly, they should be talking to their fellow CHROs or CPOs about pay and why it’s been a workplace category that hasn’t changed in decades.

“What we see is when employees feel like they’re covered, that the employer’s got their back, they feel a different connection,” Brandman said. “Suddenly you get a workforce that’s way more engaged.”

Kristin Stoller

Editorial Director, Fortune Live Media

kristin.stoller@fortune.com

Fortune Office Hours

This week, Paul Rubenstein, chief evangelist at workforce analytics software company Visier, answers your burning workplace questions. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Q: I work with a coworker who's been openly unhappy for a while, frequently complaining about where he lives, the company, and our in-office policy. He often insists that "no one comes into the office anyway," which isn't accurate. It feels like he's looking for reasons to complain.

He wants to move out of state and keep working remotely. His manager and our department head have repeatedly told him this isn't an option. He's telling coworkers he plans to move anyway but is vague with management about his actual intentions.

Yesterday, he went directly to the company president, who mistakenly assumed the move was already approved. A meeting followed where he was again told remote work wasn't an option and that skipping required office days could mean termination. He then returned to complain to the team. After he left, our department head asked the rest of us what he'd shared and how we'd feel if he were eventually allowed to work remotely. Two coworkers said they wouldn't care.

Here's where it gets complicated: I'm currently interim director, so I have management-side context my coworkers don't, even though they still treat me as a peer. So how do I stay neutral with former peers while moving into management, and am I wrong to think an exception here would reward bad behavior? How do you handle a chronically draining, disgruntled employee?

A: Your coworker handed you information you can't un-know, and then your department head asked the room a direct question. You stayed quiet. It was an awkward position to be in, but now that you’re the interim director, it's worth asking what you'd do differently next time instead of staying quiet.

You keep coming back to staying "neutral." I'd aim for clarity instead. Leadership doesn't mean picking a side in every disagreement. It means being willing to say how you see an issue and, most importantly, why. That takes vulnerability, but the payoff is lasting trust.

Your concern about making an exception is fair, too. This coworker got three clear answers and kept looking for another route while staying vague about their plans. Your team will notice what behavior gets a pass, so think about the precedent you want to set.

As for this coworker, here's the bigger question: Do you trust them? Do you respect how they operate? Those are two different things, and the answers may tell you more than whether they're simply "difficult." Think about what they bring to the team, too. Do they add energy or drain it? Life's too short to work with a Debbie Downer.

Engage this coworker by asking, “Is this how you want to show up at work?” They might not even realize what they are doing to their brand. Remember, always stick to honesty and transparency, and remember that trying to be "neutral" is a trap: It looks different for everyone depending on where you're standing.

text:
NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J. – August 24, 2026 – Johnson & Johnson today announced the publication of the DISH Classification System, a new global consensus framework developed and validated through a clinician-led initiative to standardize how surgical site outcomes are measured and reported and help bring greater visibility to underreported surgical site infections and other wound complications. Published in The British Journal of Surgery, the DISH framework provides a consistent method for identifying and grading four of the most common surgical site outcomes: dehiscence, inflammation/infection, seroma and hematoma.

Key takeaways

The DISH Classification System creates a shared language for four common surgical site outcomes: dehiscence, inflammation/infection, seroma, and hematoma.

The framework was developed through a Delphi Study and validated by clinicians globally representing over 30 countries and 14 specialties.

Grading scales support consistent documentation of management and clinical presentation.

A common language for wound outcomes enables consistent care, evidence-based treatment, and improved patient outcomes.

Wound-related complications are among the leading causes of postoperative readmission, yet a lack of standardized outcome measurement limits the ability to consistently evaluate, compare, and improve care. DISH was developed to address this gap by providing a common language for assessing surgical site outcomes beyond infection alone. Through standardized reporting and data collection, DISH creates the foundation for benchmarking outcomes, identifying best practices, and advancing evidence-based standards of care to improve patient outcomes.

“A shared language for reporting and understanding surgical outcomes is foundational for the prevention of adverse outcomes,” said Giles Bond-Smith*, MBBS, BSc, corresponding author and consultant emergency surgeon and clinical lead for surgical emergency unit at Oxford University Hospitals, NHS Foundations Trust, London, and steering committee chair for Johnson & Johnson’s Surgical Outcomes Program. “By establishing the DISH Classification System, which classifies and standardizes the definition of Dehiscence, Inflammation/Infection, Seromas and Hematomas, we now have consistent terms and an independent grading system for how a surgical site presents and how it’s managed. This makes it easier to document complications, compare clinical responses to complications across specialties, and ultimately use this data to improve patient care.”

The DISH classification system first reached a broader community of surgical experts in 2024 under the guidance of the Johnson & Johnson Surgical Outcomes Program Steering Committee, which includes Giles Bond-Smith, FRCS1; Marja A. Boermeester, MD2,3; David J Leaper, DSc4,5; Philip L. Russo, PhD6,7,8; Antonia F. Chen, MD/MBA9. Bringing together leaders across surgical specialties and healthcare disciplines, the committee sought diverse perspectives and clinical expertise around the world to advance the single, standardized framework.

“For too long, common surgical site complications have been measured differently across specialties and institutions,” said Dr. Antonia Chen**, orthopedic surgeon and steering committee member for Johnson & Johnson’s Surgical Site Outcomes Program. “DISH provides a consistent framework that can help clinicians learn from outcomes, identify opportunities for improvement, and advance patient care. As more data is collected using a common approach, we will be better positioned to understand what drives better outcomes for patients.”

The framework was refined using a modified Delphi process and the language was validated for inter and intra rater reliability across a multi-specialty cohort of over 60 clinicians. The final system includes independent scales for clinical management and clinical presentation, allowing care teams to document both how a wound was managed and what was observed without prescribing treatment pathways.

“Surgeons and care teams have asked for a clear, practical system to classify surgery-related complications and patient outcomes,” said Nisha Johnson, Global President, Wound Closure & Healing, MedTech, Johnson & Johnson. “The publication of these consensus-driven findings in The British Journal of Surgery and Johnson & Johnson’s leadership in convening this Delphi Panel of global experts reflects our commitment to advancing meaningful innovation in the OR and beyond by listening to clinicians and partnering to improve patient outcomes.”

What's the deal? Amazon Web Services (AWS), OpenAI, and Microsoft are all investing heavily in Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs) — specialists who embed directly with customers to move AI systems from prototype into production. The push signals a bet that enterprises need hands-on help to make AI actually work inside their operations.

Who's spending what? AWS has announced a $1 billion investment in a dedicated organisation intended to embed thousands of engineers with customers. OpenAI has set up a dedicated Deployment Company and agreed to acquire Tomoro, adding roughly 150 FDEs and deployment specialists. Microsoft, according to CNBC, plans to hire 6,000 people and invest $3.5 billion in a new AI delivery unit.

What do FDEs actually do? They embed with a customer, work across teams, and identify a high-value workflow before building the integrations to take a system into production. For AI, that means more than connecting a model to an app — it involves data quality, accuracy thresholds, guardrails, security, and fitting into existing business processes.

Why now? Enterprises want to run probabilistic AI systems — which can respond differently each time — inside business processes that depend on predictable, uniform results. FDEs translate those outputs into something reliable enough for real operations.

What could go wrong? A technically impressive model can still fail inside a real workflow, whether from incomplete context, poor data, or an organisation unwilling to let the system act without review. If every deployment stays bespoke and dependent on individual talent, the technology itself cannot scale.

What's the endgame? The best FDEs convert lessons from one customer into reusable connectors, evaluation frameworks, and governance patterns others can use. As Acceldata chief marketing officer Mahesh Kumar frames it, the goal is to make each deployment less dependent on any specific engineer and instead make the product better.

The signal: The FDE surge points to a new kind of hybrid professional — one who writes production software, understands AI's limits, learns a customer's business, and navigates security and governance all at once. The billions flowing into these teams suggest the industry now sees deployment, not the model itself, as the hard part of enterprise AI.

U.S. consumers are pulling back on spending in several areas, but food delivery remains a relatively resilient part of household budgets.

DoorDash Inc. (NASDAQ:DASH), Uber Technologies Inc. (NYSE:UBER) through Uber Eats and Maplebear Inc. (NASDAQ:CART), which operates Instacart, all posted strong sales growth in their latest quarterly results, showing consumers are still willing to pay for delivered restaurant meals and groceries, Business Insider reported Sunday.

DoorDash CEO Tony Xu has been surprised by consumers’ willingness to continue paying for delivery despite higher costs.

DoorDash CFO Ravi Inukonda said the broader food category remains resilient because people eat regularly, noting that "People eat 21 times a week, whether it’s food or groceries," according to the report.

Consumers Cut Back Elsewhere

Broader spending data points to a more cautious consumer. U.S. retail sales fell 0.6% in July, while Walmart posted its slowest quarterly comparable-sales growth since 2020.

Lower-income consumers have also become more budget-conscious as inflation continues to weigh on purchasing power. Consumer sentiment remained below pandemic-era levels in August, while inflation exceeded wage growth for the fourth consecutive month.

Real wages fell between December 2020 and 2024 for nearly 40% of workers, while higher prices continue to leave some households with less money available at the end of the month. That can push consumers to prioritize necessities and value while cutting less essential purchases.

Some diners are also moving away from McDonald’s and toward rivals such as Burger King and Chili’s, which have reported sales growth driven in part by value-focused meal deals.

The delivery apps are also expanding by reaching new customers and adding new offerings. Uber’s delivery gross bookings rose 26% during the second quarter, slightly outpacing growth in its ride-hailing business.

Convenience Keeps Winning

Food delivery can be expensive, but convenience remains a powerful reason consumers keep using it. Business Insider spoke with customers who said delivery saves time, helps them manage household responsibilities and can be worth the additional cost.

For some households, grocery delivery can also be more practical than shopping in person. One consumer said delivery was cheaper than taking public transportation to a nearby store because local convenience-store prices were higher even after delivery costs.

DoorDash is also expanding beyond traditional restaurant delivery. The company has added more stores and grocery options, including regional grocers and The Kroger Co. (NYSE:KR) purchases using SNAP benefits, giving consumers more reasons to use its platform.

Food Costs Keep Rising

The resilience of delivery comes despite continued pressure on food prices. A basic meal of a cheeseburger, fries and a drink rose 3.2% in price over the past year, with only a handful of U.S. cities averaging below $15.

Food affordability is also straining household finances. More than one-quarter of working-age adults who used credit cards for groceries either could not pay their balances in full or missed minimum payments, while about 20% said they had used long-term savings, including emergency funds, to pay for groceries.

That creates an unusual consumer picture: households are becoming more selective with spending, but food remains a necessity and convenience can still command a premium.

For delivery platforms, that could make food and grocery orders more resilient than other forms of discretionary spending, particularly as consumers look for ways to save time without cutting essential purchases entirely.

text:
Roche has taken its obesity strategy into uncharted territory via a $190 million upfront payment for a clinical-stage UCN2 (urocortin-2) analog from South Korea’s Hanmi Pharm.

UCN2 is a signalling protein that is elevated in people with chronic heart failure. The mechanism was explored by Eli Lilly in a heart failure drug that was scrapped back in 2019.

Researchers have known for decades that UCN2 can in principle reduce rates of muscle atrophy, and Roche is betting that Hanmi’s drug, dubbed HM17321, will be able to deliver on this promise.

In return for the $190 million upfront fee and the potential for up to 2.3 billion in development, regulatory and commercial milestone payments, Roche’s Genentech unit has secured the global rights to HM17321, excluding South Korea. Hanmi is also in line for tiered royalties on sales.

Reducing weight while maintaining muscle mass is one of the key goals of the next generation of obesity treatments. Roche has its own candidate in the running for this prize in the form of emugrobart, an anti-latent myostatin sweeping antibody that is designed to increase muscle mass and is undergoing a phase 2 study in combination with Lilly’s Mounjaro.

In this morning’s release, Hanmi explained that HM17321’s non-incretin mechanism of action means the therapy could become a “first-in-class treatment designed to simultaneously promote weight loss and preserve lean body mass.”

“While existing GLP-1-based incretin therapies have demonstrated meaningful weight reduction, these therapies are associated with a reduction in lean body mass,” the Korean biotech pointed out.

“The paradigm of obesity treatment is evolving beyond simple weight reduction toward improving body composition and restoring metabolic health,” In-Young Choi, head of Hanmi’s R&D division, said in the release.

“We are very pleased that the differentiated scientific mechanism and development potential of HM17321 have been recognized by the global market,” Choi added.

Roche is planning to explore HM17321’s potential to treat not only obesity but also associated conditions such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

The companies noted that HM17321 has alreay been linked to weight reduction when used as a monotherapy and in combination with GLP-1-based therapies in preclinical testing. Hanmi has since taken HM17321 into a phase 1 trial of healthy volunteers and individuals with obesity. The biotech will complete this study before Genentech takes over for phase 2 development and beyond.

Roche stepped up its obesity ambitions last year, including a bold goal of becoming one of the “top three” companies operating in the weight loss space. That strategy included an aim of taking the dual GLP-1/GIP receptor enicepatide to market by 2030.

There’s also another Carmot asset in phase 2 studies in the form of an oral GLP-1 dubbed CT-996. Then there’s petrelintide, Zealand Pharma’s long-acting amylin analog that Roche is partnering on.

“With our growing cardiometabolic pipeline and strong diagnostic expertise, Roche is advancing a portfolio designed to meet the diverse needs of people living with obesity and related health conditions,” Head of Roche Corporate Business Development Boris Zaïtra said in the release.

“By licensing this next-generation investigational therapy with first-in-class potential from Hanmi, Roche and Genentech will pursue a differentiated approach to selectively reduce fat mass while improving both muscle mass and muscle function,” Zaïtra added.

text:
For the last two years, contractors working for Walmart have used 3D-printed construction at a handful of sites across the U.S. The walls for five additions to existing stores in Tennessee, Missouri, Alabama, and Arkansas have been completed in this fashion so far. It’s the country’s largest deployment of 3D-printed architecture in the commercial sector. The retailer’s scale is catalyzing the growth and adoption of the technology, which promises to construct buildings faster and more affordably.

Digital fabrication meets big-box stores

The use of 3D printing for construction has mostly focused on residential structures, owing to their smaller size and the nascent state of the technology. Expanding 3D printing to the commercial sector could help scale up the industry. Meanwhile, completing larger structures with bigger budgets could help prove the utility of the process—and even help bend the cost curve.

To complete its 3D-printed builds, Walmart partnered with Alquist, the maker of robotic A1X 3D printers, and FMGI, a longtime contractor of the Arkansas-based retail giant. (Walmart declined the opportunity to comment on this story.)

“This is what keeps me excited,” says Darin Ross, the president and CEO of FMGI, which is based in Woodstock, Georgia. He founded his company in his basement and as it grew into a nationwide firm, he eagerly awaited more innovation. “For 30 years, I’ve watched the construction industry just do it the same way over and over,” he says. “We as an industry are way behind in adopting new technology and new ways of doing things.”

FMGI is trained to operate Alquist’s 3D printers—which pipe layers of a concrete composite, like toothpaste being squeezed from a tube—and recently agreed to expand an existing arrangement with Walmart to 3D print buildings. This includes full-scale buildings and 30-plus projects in the pipeline through 2027.

The partnership started with a pilot build at Walmart’s Athens, Tennessee, location in September 2024. Alquist printers laid out the walls for an 8,000-square-foot, 20-foot-high expansion of the superstore. The additional area helped the store to better accommodate increased pickup and delivery traffic. At that time, it was the largest 3D-printed commercial structure in the United States.

title: Lilly, Novo Amp Up GLP-1 Fight With New Weapon Against Copycats - Bloomberg Law
description:
Eli Lilly & Co. and Novo Nordisk A/S are leveraging a fresh weapon in their crackdown against copycat versions of their blockbuster weight loss drugs.
The latest endeavor has so far proven successful as compounders have voluntarily discontinued or modified disputed claims.
The stakes are clear: Lilly’s tirzepatide and Novo’s semaglutide are among the only FDA-cleared GLP-1 drugs.
While the NAD doesn’t hold any legal authority, it can escalate the matter to regulators such as the FDA, Federal Trade Commission, or state attorneys general for potential enforcement.

text:
Eli Lilly & Co. and Novo Nordisk A/S are leveraging a fresh weapon in their crackdown against copycat versions of their blockbuster weight loss drugs.

The two pharmaceutical giants over the last year have filed 10 cases against compounders and telehealth companies with BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division, a self-regulatory body providing dispute resolution over advertising claims. The non-government group has been around since 1971, settling disagreements over products from bathroom cleaners to infant formula — but the GLP-1 drugmakers turned to it relatively recently.

It’s another avenue in the aggressive fight to rein in unapproved versions of their powerful obesity and diabetes GLP-1 drugs, adding to a string of federal lawsuits and cease-and-desist letters filed against copycats in the last two years. The latest endeavor has so far proven successful as compounders have voluntarily discontinued or modified disputed claims.

The stakes are clear: Lilly’s tirzepatide and Novo’s semaglutide are among the only FDA-cleared GLP-1 drugs. Lilly’s franchise reached $40 billion in sales, while Novo’s products generated $35 billion last year.

“They’re using a lot of arsenals,” said Alan Minsk, chair of the food and drug practice at Arnall Golden Gregory LLP. “These are big bucks for the companies and they’re trying to use all of their tools that they’ve got.”

The series of challenges largely began after the FDA determined that branded GLP-1s are now available following a shortage period, effectively prohibiting mass production of cheaper copies that have been used by at least a million patients. Still, compounders continue to make personalized versions.

“We will continue to work with law enforcement and regulators to help address illegal activity,” a Novo spokesperson said in an email, sharing the company has filed 130 federal lawsuits and five challenges with the NAD. “Novo Nordisk views NAD challenges as an important forum to bring complaints against companies making false and misleading claims about unapproved compounded drugs.”

Lilly, which has also filed dozens of federal lawsuits and at least five cases with the NAD, similarly credited the division as “an independent authority whose mission is to build consumer trust in advertising.”

Each company challenged by Novo or Lilly did not respond to requests for comment.

Speedier Pathway

The forum has long served as a faster and more cost-effective process compared to litigation, which can drag on for years.

Unlike legal proceedings, the burden is on the defendant, or the advertiser, to demonstrate it has a reasonable basis to make the claim at issue. The division assigns an attorney to review a case, confer with parties for a briefing period, and ultimately draft a decision or recommendation.

The process, however, is voluntary. Companies can file a challenge, but an advertiser isn’t required to participate in the case or follow recommendations. While the NAD doesn’t hold any legal authority, it can escalate the matter to regulators such as the FDA, Federal Trade Commission, or state attorneys general for potential enforcement. It may also report the ad to social media platforms where it runs.

“It’s been interesting to see this case package come from the GLP-1 manufacturers,” Phyllis Marcus, vice president of the NAD. “They present almost the full suite of advertising techniques. You’ve got social media, you’ve got influencers, you’ve got health claims, you’ve got one of the hottest drugs on the market.”

Advertisers can appeal decisions to a board of academics and brand representatives.

“The options vary a lot in terms of cost, timeframe to a resolution, and effectiveness,” said Ricardo Carvajal, a director at Hyman, Phelps & McNamara P.C., representing advertisers. “But at the end of the day, we’re talking about a matter of months to get to a final resolution in the form of an NAD case decision.”

Lilly’s latest challenge targeted Noom Inc.’s “A Smaller Dose. A Smarter Start” tagline for its compounded GLP-1s. The NAD determined the company failed to provide adequate support for its message. Noom disagreed with the conclusion but still agreed to drop or modify the claim.

Novo’s latest case pressured Willow Health Services Inc. to permanently discontinue certain safety and efficacy claims for its compounded semaglutide. The move came after the NAD referred the matter to the FTC and state attorneys general when Willow failed to provide a statement indicating whether it would comply with recommendations.

Seeking Enforcement

The rise in challenges comes amid a lighter regulatory touch from the FDA.

“FDA is likely receiving many trade complaints,” said Dara Katcher Levy, a director at Hyman, counseling companies on product communications. “That’s probably why companies are now moving toward the NAD option of bringing their complaints. FDA’s warning letters, at least in this space for the telehealth and compounders, have been very narrow.”

While compounded drug ads can’t be false or misleading under federal laws, they still don’t face the same kind of government sign-off as brand-name treatments. Still, the FDA has increasingly targeted them in the last year with more than 100 warning letters sent to companies regarding misbranded claims.

But even with increased oversight, the FDA’s warnings have largely focused on a limited set of claims such as active ingredients, branding, and product performance.

title: Biopharma's selective recovery: Differentiation and strategic clarity define success
description:
The biopharma sector is experiencing what Clark describes as a "selective recovery" rather than a broad market reopening.
As CEO of strategic communications firm Optimum, she has a front-row seat to the conversations shaping the industry.
"Across financing, licensing and M&A, we're seeing larger deals, bigger deals, concerning a smaller number of companies," Clark explained.
The strongest partners now show clear alignment in science, the development path, the market opportunity and the needs of potential partners."
"Companies need credible science, a clear strategic fit and a convincing explanation of why their opportunity matters now.
text:
The biopharma sector is experiencing what Clark describes as a "selective recovery" rather than a broad market reopening. As CEO of strategic communications firm Optimum, she has a front-row seat to the conversations shaping the industry. Clark sat down with BioXconomy ahead of BIO-Europe in Cologne, Germany, to discuss her overview of the industry.

Her assessment is clear: capital is flowing, deal activity is robust and initial public offering (IPO) windows are opening, but only for companies that can demonstrate clear differentiation, credible execution and a compelling rationale for why they matter now.

"I am pretty positive," Clark said when asked to characterize the current market environment in 2026. "The market is definitely more selective and more demanding, but it's rewarding companies that can show clear differentiation, credible execution and a strong rationale for why they matter now."

The numbers support her optimism. Year-to-date data for 2026 paints a picture of concentrated activity and purposeful decision-making. In the first half of the year, biopharma venture funding reached approximately $16.3 billion across 235 rounds, while biopharma IPOs raised around $5 billion across 13 offerings, already surpassing the full-year totals seen from 2022 to 2025. Announced research and development licensing value reached roughly $166.7 billion, and biopharma mergers and acquisitions (M&A’s) totalled around $96 billion across 80 deals, including 33 transactions valued at $1 billion or more.

"The stats on the number of deals being done, financing, IPOs, are all fantastic and better than the previous years," Clark noted enthusiastically. "M&A is definitely notable in terms of the deals being done and the size of the deals being done, in really specific areas like precision oncology and immunology."

Activity has concentrated in oncology, immunology and other strategically important therapeutic areas. This includes high-profile transactions such as GSK's acquisition of Nuvalent in precision oncology, AbbVie's purchase of Apogee in immunology, Gilead's acquisition of Arcellx in cell therapy, and multiple Eli Lilly acquisitions across areas such as Centessa Pharmaceuticals and Kelonia Therapeutics.

Clark is particularly excited about Novartis' proposed acquisition of UK-based Myricx Bio, backed by Sofinnova, for up to $1.5 billion to strengthen its antibody drug conjugate (ADC) platform in oncology. "Just brilliant," she said. "It strengthens ADCs and the power of that modality."

"Across financing, licensing and M&A, we're seeing larger deals, bigger deals, concerning a smaller number of companies," Clark explained. "We're seeing capital and pharma attention around differentiated, late-stage assets with clear pathways."

This selectivity has profound implications for how companies communicate their value proposition. Clark argued that the bar has been raised significantly, and companies can no longer rely solely on strong science to capture attention and capital.

"From a communications perspective, that raises the bar," she told us. "Companies need to show not just strong science, but why the opportunity matters now, how it fits investor and pharma opportunities, and how it can create durable value in a more disciplined market."

For leadership teams, the fundamental question has evolved. "It's no longer a question of how we progress this program," Clark emphasized. "It's how can we make a compelling case for why this matters, why now, and why we are the right team to deliver it. The stronger stories connect science to unmet needs, strategic relevance, commercial logic and long-term value creation."

In what Clark described as a hugely competitive market for deals, for people and for finance, companies have got to make sure their story is being heard at the right time and by the right audiences.

Partnering as strategic imperative

The role of partnering within the industry has also evolved significantly. Partnering has always been important, Clark acknowledged, but before it was perhaps more about business development momentum, capital flow and deal access. Partnering is now much more closely tied to strategic fit, risk-sharing with partners and long-term portfolio planning.

"We have the backdrop of regulatory complexity, patent cliffs, artificial intelligence (AI), manufacturing and cross-border sourcing," she said. "And again, that changes the communications side. Why is it compelling? The strongest partners now show clear alignment in science, the development path, the market opportunity and the needs of potential partners."

One notable trend is the continuing flow of China-origin licensing deals into Western pharma, where companies are often buying global or ex-China rights to clinically promising assets while using milestone-heavy structures to manage risk. This shift changes the communications challenge fundamentally.

In an increasingly complex environment, leadership teams are making decisions across multiple dimensions simultaneously: scientific validity, financing options, partner appetite, development risk, commercial positioning and stakeholder expectations. Clark argued communications become a key part of the strategic decision-making process.

"What is the priority? What is differentiated? What matters most to stakeholders? What evidence do we have to support the story?" Clark asked. "It's not enough to explain the science. Companies also need to explain: Why this indication? Why you as the partner? Why this financing route? Why this timing? What's beneficial now?"

Clark discussed how one of the biggest risks is fragmented messaging. This is where scientific teams, commercial teams, business development teams and investor-facing teams all tell slightly different versions of the story. "When we have a complex and fragmented market, it's all about what your interpretation and understanding is. In this market, consistency and coherence is a strategic advantage," she said.

The value of industry dialogue

In a fragmented market, shared industry conversations play an increasingly important role in shaping sentiment, priorities and ultimately decision-making across the sector. Clark sees significant value in shared interpretation.

"Industry dialogue makes companies understand how they are going to be perceived, what's happening in the sector, what the concerns are, what is gaining credibility. It means companies need to engage much more."

This means companies need the same strategy across events and outside of the company.

Europe's convening role

Clark described how she believes that Europe has a real opportunity to act as a neutral convening ground for biopharma stakeholders.

"With lots happening in the world, Europe offers a trusted place, a setting where global players can meet on equal footing," she explained. "It's not that we're going to replace other hubs, but we can connect US, European and international perspectives. This is a time where we need to share more openly and discuss more freely in the sector."

When asked what the industry is looking for today from its major conferences, Clark's answer was straightforward.

"Major conferences now need to provide useful insights as much as deal flow," she said. "Leaders want forums to test assumptions, understand where consensus is forming and leave with a clear view of where to focus next."

The most useful conversations are often not just the scheduled partnering meetings, but the panels, side meetings and informal discussions that reveal where investor appetite, pharma priorities and policy concerns are starting to align. The strongest platforms are those that bring together the full value chain: biotech, pharma, investors, policymakers, service providers and others who influence how innovation moves forward.

“For Optimum, we know capital is there, partnering is active, M&A is clearly happening and moving, but the bar is higher," she concluded. "Companies need credible science, a clear strategic fit and a convincing explanation of why their opportunity matters now. That's why good communications and the right industry forums really matter. They help leaders read the signals, build confidence and focus on the decisions that will create value."

text:
Dubai has adopted a unified Workforce Productivity Measurement System across its government, with the technology now implemented in 32 government entities and using machine learning and advanced artificial intelligence to support analysis and decision-making.

The Dubai Government Human Resources Department (DGHR) said the system was developed over five years and draws on millions of data points to measure workforce productivity, improve resource allocation and provide government entities with insights for planning and policy development.

The system was formally adopted as a government-wide framework under Executive Council Resolution No. 67 of 2025.

Its implementation is intended to support Dubai’s broader shift towards data-driven government, creating a unified methodology for measuring productivity and analyzing the relationship between human and financial resources, government outputs and service outcomes.

According to DGHR, the system incorporates analytical tools and digital platforms powered by machine learning and AI, allowing government entities to monitor productivity indicators and assess how resources are being used.

The resulting data is intended to support more efficient planning, improve institutional performance and provide policymakers with more accurate and forward-looking insights.

Development of the system began in 2020 with a pilot involving a limited number of government entities. During the project phase, the Workforce Productivity Measurement Steering Committee was established under Resolution No. 7 of 2023 to help develop the methodology and prepare entities for wider implementation.

Following the system’s government-wide adoption, the committee concluded its work after completing its assigned responsibilities.

Abdullah Ali Bin Zayed Al Falasi, Director General of DGHR, said the adoption of the system marked a step in Dubai’s efforts to build a government increasingly driven by data and advanced analytics.

“The adoption of the Workforce Productivity Measurement System across the Government of Dubai represents a strategic milestone in the advancement of government work and reflects Dubai’s vision to build a government driven by data and advanced analytics,” Al Falasi said.

He added that the system goes beyond measuring productivity by establishing a unified framework to support resource allocation, improve service quality and strengthen institutional performance.

The initiative forms part of Dubai’s wider efforts to use data and digital technologies to improve government operations, with the system designed to help entities make more efficient use of resources while supporting policy development and service delivery.
